title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to test whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered guarded exclusions changes validator‑measured success rates. Execution artifacts show the sample used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). Because of these executed choices, no preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags occurred and baseline and guarded validator pass counts were identical (150/150 each). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Crucially, we explicitly reclassify the prespecified primary confirmatory test as degenerate for this execution (artifact evidence below), diagnose why the preregistration→execution mismatch produced an uninformative null, and provide artifact‑grounded recommendations (provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation, full per‑item overlap persistence, multi‑model replication, paraphrase‑sensitive detectors) to increase audit sensitivity in future runs. All reported numbers and artifacts are archived and cited in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Motivation and questions. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and automated configuration repair. When benchmark evidence informs operational trust, auditors must rule out dataset contamination (items or templates present in model training corpora) and construct invalidity (excessly templated tasks that overstate capability). We preregistered an artifact‑anchored confirmatory audit to ask: under conservative deterministic detectors and a guarded exclusion policy, (1) how many high‑confidence contamination flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item sample and (2) how much does applying those controls change a single hosted LLM's validator pass rate? Study_id: contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1.

Contributions and high‑level outcome. We provide (1) a fully preregistered execution archived with validator traces and execution manifests; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory counts for N_pairs = 150 (baseline_success = 150, guarded_success = 150; n11 = 150); and (3) an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation that documents why the executed configuration (provenance‑stable synthetic sampling + shared_initial_candidate generation) rendered the primary paired test uninformative. From artifact evidence we derive concrete, implementable design changes for contamination audits of web‑sourced benchmarks.

Scope and inference bounds. The preregistration targeted four public benchmark identifiers (benchmark_scope: https://openalex.org/W7157506260, https://openalex.org/W4404602270, https://openalex.org/W4404534210, https://openalex.org/W7166900660). The executed run instead sampled deterministic synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") using deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (see execution/task_manifest.jsonl; hash b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55). Because the executed sample and generation semantics are archived, the observed null applies only to this synthetic, shared‑generation regime and does not indicate absence of contamination in independent web‑sourced benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑for‑NetOps and validators. Prior system and benchmark work shows LLMs can produce intent→configuration artifacts and propose repairs, and that integrating verifiers or iterative validate–repair loops improves average repair quality [https://openalex.org/W7157506260; https://openalex.org/W7162218766]. Deterministic/formal verification tools (Header Space Analysis and related approaches) serve as practical oracles for reachability and policy checks and are commonly used in generate–validate pipelines [http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.300.8659; https://openalex.org/W2742515467].

Contamination and evaluation validity. Recent surveys and framework proposals document two recurring evaluation risks—contamination and construct invalidity—and recommend deterministic fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, provenance tracing, and transparent reporting of detector outputs to mitigate inflated performance claims [https://openalex.org/W4404534210; https://openalex.org/W7166900660]. Our work implements a conservative subset of these defenses in a preregistered confirmatory setting and contributes an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of when those defenses are uninformative given execution semantics.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen analysis plan. The experiment was preregistered (contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) and froze: the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), sample size (task_count = 150), detector definitions (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80), exclusion/replacement rules (exclude high‑confidence flags only), and the analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 (exact McNemar two‑sided primary test; paired bootstrap percentile CI with 10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Planned maximum_model_calls = 300 (baseline+guarded independent generations) but the preregistration permitted deterministic shared generation to reduce provider calls; the preregistered execution contract documented both options.

Sampling and deterministic generation. For reproducibility we permitted deterministic synthetic task generation. The executed run used deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and produced task_manifest entries with source_identifier values beginning "synthetic-netops:" (artifact: execution/task_manifest.jsonl; hash b7c08599...). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, and explicit workflow constraints. The preregistration allowed both independent_condition_generation (two separate generations per item) and shared_initial_candidate semantics; the executed model_configuration.json records independent_condition_generation = false (shared generation semantics) (artifact: execution/model_configuration.json; hash a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820).

Contamination detectors and persistence behavior. The preregistered detector suite implemented: (1) exact normalized token equality; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered thresholds (high confidence ≥ 0.80; sensitivity brackets at 0.65 and 0.50); and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics. The detector workflow was implemented to persist full per‑item fuzzy overlap tables only when thresholds or replacements were invoked; this persistence policy is recorded in the transformation manifest (execution/transformation_manifest.json) and explains why a global per‑item overlap table is absent from the archive when no threshold crossings occurred. The contamination_summary artifact (analysis/contamination_summary.csv; hash 389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222) contains any flagged rows—none were produced in this execution.

Guarded policy, replacements, and validation oracle. The preregistered guarded policy deterministically excluded only high‑confidence flagged items (exact match OR 5‑gram ≥ 0.80) and deterministically replaced them via retemplating/topology augmentation with fixed seeds; replacements required an embedding similarity safeguard (cosine ≥ 0.85) before acceptance. No high‑confidence flags occurred; thus no replacements were performed. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) served as the binary oracle (full_intent_constraint_validation): parse→state_update→property checks (final state equality on allowed fields and workflow constraint adherence). Validator traces (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes) were archived per episode (execution/scoring/*.json; representative examples in manuscript bundle).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciliation. Execution completed planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 item pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false the pipeline performed a single shared generation per item and reused that candidate for both baseline and guarded episodes when no exclusions occurred; provider accounting records model_calls_used = 150 (artifact: deterministic_reconciliation.json; hash 57c70942a9ffa93f7a2cb0c87c8996fcf12d516066a3ce6b5dcbb33add40b8b8). The reduced model_calls_used relative to the preregistered maximum is an executed choice recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (hash a40e96e2...).

Contamination detectors: no preregistered high‑confidence flags. The detector workflow produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed sample; analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty of flagged rows (artifact hash 389227f0...). As implemented, detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs were persisted only on threshold crossings or replacements (see execution/transformation_manifest.json); therefore, no global overlap distribution file exists in the archive for this run and per‑item overlap reconstruction is not possible from the provided artifacts.

Validator outcomes and primary statistics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table (artifact: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; hash c2ba9cdb5d0938eae910129ba511eadf309319e6e05b36d9e3b4860032deb80e) is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Hence the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All per‑episode raw responses and validator traces are archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl; hash 5337998d1d86aca507f77659d75cc9487cf3d87a157ed5044b8a9d5ff79b5586) and underpin these numbers.

Representative episode diagnostic. Representative archived episode pair-000001 (task-000001) shows identical normalized_response and normalized_reference_answer and validator fields: parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, score = 1 (VALID_CONFIGURATION). That exemplar and similar episode traces are included in the execution bundle to validate scorer semantics (see execution/scoring/*.json artifacts).
sections.discussion:
Why the prespecified primary test is degenerate here. The preregistered primary confirmatory hypothesis H2 (that guarded exclusions reduce measured success) was rendered untestable for this execution because two jointly archived execution facts collapsed the paired comparison: (A) the confirmatory sample was drawn from deterministic synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (artifact: execution/task_manifest.jsonl; hash b7c08599...), and (B) the pipeline used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false; artifact: execution/model_configuration.json; hash a40e96e2...), meaning a single model generation per item was reused for both baseline and guarded episodes when no exclusions occurred. Under these conditions, baseline vs guarded discordance depends solely on flagged‑driven replacements; with zero high‑confidence flags the pairwise outcomes are mechanically identical (n11 = 150). We therefore reclassify the primary test as degenerate for the executed run and present the observed concordance as a mechanistic diagnostic outcome rather than evidence that contamination is absent in web‑sourced benchmarks.

Missing per‑item overlap scores and interpretability consequences. The detector persistence policy (execution/transformation_manifest.json) archived detailed fuzzy overlap outputs only for threshold crossings or replacements; because none occurred no per‑item overlap table was written and analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty (artifact hash 389227f0...). This absence is an explicit artifact of the detector implementation, not a silent omission: it prevents post‑hoc inspection of how close items came to the 0.80 threshold (e.g., whether max overlaps were 0.10 or 0.60). To improve interpretability, future runs should persist all per‑item overlap scores unconditionally.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations to make audits sensitive to public‑benchmark contamination. The archive supports the following concrete changes: (1) sample provenance‑rich public items (URLs/DOIs and timestamps present) rather than synthetic items to enable meaningful provenance heuristics; (2) set independent_condition_generation = true to obtain independent baseline and guarded generations per item (increasing model_calls_used and observable discordance); (3) persist full per‑item fuzzy overlap scores (analysis/contamination_scores.csv) irrespective of threshold crossings; (4) expand to multiple model instances and independent seeds to improve power and cross‑model signal; (5) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and small human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows directly from explicit gaps visible in the current archive: model_calls_used = 150 (deterministic_reconciliation.json; hash 57c70942...), empty contamination_summary.csv (hash 389227f0...), and absence of a global overlap table.

Operational implications and cautions. The archived validator traces demonstrate that generate–validate pipelines produce precise, inspectable evidence of functional correctness for the checked constraints. However, auditors and practitioners must avoid extrapolating this synthetic shared‑generation null to public benchmarks: the present run documents only that, in a provenance‑stable synthetic sample with shared generation semantics, conservative lexical detectors produced no high‑confidence flags and thus no guarded effect. Detecting contamination in web‑sourced corpora requires the recommended changes above.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored audit of deterministic contamination detectors in an LLM‑for‑NetOps setting. The executed sample and generation semantics (synthetic provenance + shared_initial_candidate) produced zero high‑confidence flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline and guarded). We explicitly reclassify the prespecified primary confirmatory test as degenerate for this execution and provide an artifact‑grounded reconciliation explaining why. To make paired contamination audits informative for public benchmarks, future preregistered runs should sample provenance‑rich public items, use independent generation per condition, persist full per‑item overlap scores, expand to multi‑model replication, and incorporate paraphrase‑sensitive detection plus human adjudication. All numbers and traces reported here are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement below.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here does not imply absence of contamination in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative lexical heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
